stops.title: The question
stops.text: MiniMind-O showed you an omni model small enough to build from scratch. Now let's look at a full-size one. Qwen2.5-Omni asks whether a single open model can read text, images, audio and video together, and answer both in writing and in natural speech, while you are still talking. For a text, image and voice project this is the easy case: all three input types are native. So as we go, watch where each modality enters, and which part you would actually fine-tune.

stops.title: Every input, one brain
stops.text: Here is the whole model on one page. Text goes through a byte-level tokenizer, images and video through one shared vision transformer, and voice through an audio encoder that starts from Whisper. Every lane ends as tokens for the same language model, which the paper calls the Thinker. On the right, a second decoder called the Talker turns the Thinker's thoughts into speech. Notice what is missing: the model cannot generate images or video. And notice what you do not need: a separate speech recognizer.

stops.title: Why it is hard
stops.text: Why not just glue encoders onto a language model? The paper names three problems. First, if you simply line up video tokens and then audio tokens, the picture and the sound from the same second end up far apart, and the model loses the connection. Second, one decoder asked to write text and speech at once gets two training signals pulling against each other. Third, every stage adds delay before the user hears anything. Each of the next stops answers one of these.

stops.title: Thinker and Talker
stops.text: The answer to interference is to split the work. The Thinker writes text. The Talker speaks, and it gets two inputs. The Thinker's hidden states carry meaning and tone, so speech can start before the sentence is finished. But hidden states group words by meaning, not by sound, so the Talker also gets the sampled text tokens to pin down pronunciation. The two parts are still trained end to end, as one model, with no word-level alignment between text and audio.

stops.title: What gets trained when
stops.text: This timeline matters for your fine-tuning plan. In stage one the language model is frozen, shown in grey, while the adapters and then the encoders learn to talk to it. In stage two everything is unfrozen and trained on more than a trillion image, audio and video tokens. Stage three stretches the context to about thirty-two thousand tokens. Then the Talker gets its own three stages, including a preference step that rewards clean, well-paused speech. You will do the reverse: freeze the encoders, adapt the language model.

stops.title: One clock for sound and sight
stops.text: The fix for synchronisation is TMRoPE. Every token gets three position numbers: time, height and width. Audio tokens move one time step every forty milliseconds, so twenty-five steps make a second. A video frame's tokens all share the time step of that frame, and spread out in height and width. So a frame and the sound heard at the same moment get the same time number. The video is then fed in two second chunks, pictures first, then their audio.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: Here is the result I want you to remember. The gold bars are Qwen2.5-Omni answering spoken questions, the indigo bars a text model answering the same questions typed. They are close, and on grade-school maths the spoken version even wins. The older audio model in grey is far behind. On the mixed benchmark OmniBench it also leads clearly. The caveat: on some tasks, like the Chinese exam set, speaking the question still costs a lot. That gap is something you can measure yourself.

stops.title: What you take from it
stops.text: So how do you use this in your own fine-tuning project? You do not need a speech-to-text step, though Whisper makes a fair baseline. Check memory first: load the smallest checkpoint in four bits, switch off speech output, keep clips short, and put LoRA on the Thinker's attention and feed-forward layers only. Copy the paper's chat format for your data, and test typed against spoken questions, and one language or accent against another. Next, Qwen3-Omni shows where this same team took the design one generation later.
